sections.h2: City certificate required before a sale
sections.html:
Miami Gardens requires a Certificate of Re-Occupancy before a property is purchased, sold, conveyed or transferred. That city step comes before closing, so build it into your timeline from day one. It takes five to seven business days when all information is provided, and it applies to every kind of sale, retail or investor. Its purpose is to help the city track changes to structures.

  • Ask for the certificate early, before a contract deadline forces a scramble.
  • Gather the permits for past repairs and upgrades.
  • Ask the city whether open violations or liens are recorded against the parcel.

The owner applies through the city's code enforcement and business licensing office, reachable at reoccupancy@miamigardens-fl.gov. The city inspects for changes made without a permit, and altered space such as added square footage is reported to the county so the property record and taxes can be corrected.

Violations do not stop a sale. It can go ahead as long as the buyer signs a stipulation agreement with the city promising to fix the problems. That helps with tired houses, since a buyer willing to cure the violations can still close.

Unpermitted work is handled by legalizing it, which means securing a permit after the fact. That can bring penalties and, in the worst case, demolition of the structure, so find out before you list.

Miami Gardens steps before a sale
TopicWhat the city requires
Certificate of Re-OccupancyRequired before purchase, sale, conveyance or transfer of title; 5 to 7 business days when information is complete
Unpermitted workMust be legalized by securing a permit
Open violationsSale can proceed if the buyer signs a stipulation agreement with the city
Landlord PermitRenewable each year on or before March 31
LiensLien searches, administrative release, and lien amnesty or reduction

The city lists fences, hurricane shutters, door and window installations, sheds, screen enclosures, pool barriers, patio slabs, gazebos, plumbing and electrical work, air conditioner change-outs, room additions and sea walls. The list is not complete, so call the building department before assuming anything is exempt.

If you replaced an air conditioner, enclosed a patio or put up a shed, dig out the permit papers now. Gaps in that record are a likely reason an inspection drags on.

Yard and street rules can also draw citations before a sale. Open-air storage is prohibited, portable storage containers should be removed within thirty calendar days, and vehicles on the swale or public right of way may be towed. Clear those items before an inspector or buyer visits.

A rented house needs a Landlord Permit, renewable every year by March 31. The application needs the permit fee, the names and birthdates of all occupants, and a national background check for occupants aged 15 and over.

A sitting tenant changes the sale. Florida's demand for unpaid rent runs 3 days, leaving out weekends and court holidays, and a monthly tenancy ends on 30 days' notice. After a court win, the sheriff restores possession once a 24-hour notice has been posted.

An investor may want the house empty, may keep the tenant, or may ask you to deliver it vacant. Write that choice into the contract so nobody guesses at closing.

Miami Gardens lies inside Miami-Dade, so the county's own deed stamp applies: 60 cents per $100, plus a 45 cent surtax that a single-family-only transfer does not owe.

The clerk takes the tax at recording, and each signer shares liability. Warranty, special warranty, quit claim and trustee's deeds are all taxable, as is a deed given to a lender instead of foreclosure. Recording is priced per page under section 28.24, with added trust fund and technology charges.

Miami-Dade's appraiser values the parcel and the county's tax collector issues the bill. The appraiser mails no bills and sets no taxes. Its 2026 roll was certified on October 16, 2026.

The calendar starts with a January 1 valuation date and a March 1 exemption deadline, then proposed notices in August and bills in November. Late bills turn delinquent in April, and tax certificates follow by June.

After a sale the buyer is assessed at full value from the next New Year's Day, and your homestead exemption stops. If you buy elsewhere in Florida, ask about portability, requested with the new homestead filing.

  • Have the closing agent prorate this year's bill between you and the buyer.
  • Check that no tax certificate has been sold against the parcel.
  • Ask the appraiser whether a city inspection changed the property record.

sections.h2: What if the house is in foreclosure or probate?
sections.html:
Foreclosure follows the court's calendar. The clerk schedules the sale 20 to 35 days after final judgment unless the lender agrees to wait, and after a sale homeowners should ask the clerk about surplus funds.

An inherited house may qualify for Florida's summary administration, which fits estates of up to $150,000 in non-exempt property or deaths over two years old. Creditors lose their claims after a statutory window that runs from the notice to creditors or from service on a known creditor.

Ask a Florida attorney or the clerk's self-help staff which papers a title insurer will require before it covers the sale.

sections.h2: City liens on a Miami Gardens house
sections.html:
The city's code compliance team offers a lien resolution service with four parts: lien searches, administrative release of a lien, lien amnesty and lien reduction, and registration of vacant and abandoned property through a third party.

Order a lien search early. A fine that has piled up from an old violation is the kind of surprise that shows up on a title report days before closing. If a lien exists, ask the city whether amnesty or reduction applies, and get the release in writing so the title company can record it.

Owners of a vacant house should also ask about vacant property registration, since an empty, neglected house draws code attention. Mow, secure and clear the yard before a buyer or inspector visits.

Total up the cash you would keep after every cost, then read who handles the re-occupancy certificate, any city lien payoff and the deed stamp. An as-is investor should still state in writing who pays city fees and who signs the stipulation agreement.

Before signing, get the settlement date, the closing agent's name and the deposit terms in writing.

Plan the order of steps: request the certificate and a lien search first, fix or disclose violations, then sign the contract and deed. Doing the city steps first keeps the closing date from slipping, and it gives the buyer a clear picture of what is left to fix.

faqs.q: Is a city certificate needed to transfer a Miami Gardens house?
faqs.a: Yes. A Certificate of Re-Occupancy is required before the purchase, sale, conveyance or transfer of title of any real property, with a turnaround of five to seven business days when information is complete.

faqs.q: May a Miami Gardens house with open violations be sold?
faqs.a: Yes, when the buyer signs a stipulation agreement promising the city to fix them. Unpermitted work must be legalized through a permit.

faqs.q: When is the Miami Gardens landlord permit due?
faqs.a: It renews each year on or before March 31. The application needs the fee, all occupants' names and birthdates and a national background check for occupants aged 15 and over.

faqs.q: What deed stamp tax applies in Miami Gardens?
faqs.a: Miami-Dade uses 60 cents per $100 and a 45 cent surtax, and a deed moving only a single-family home owes no surtax.

faqs.q: Which office mails Miami Gardens property tax bills?
faqs.a: The Miami-Dade tax collector. The property appraiser assesses value and neither mails bills nor collects taxes.
